item.title: Field Notes on Reliable Agents (6): Re-Verify the Old Fixes Every Round
item.description: If you run a system in a continuous improvement loop — round after round of “find something to make better, change it, verify, repeat” — you eventually hit a specific, demoralizing failure: a change in round 20 quietly re-breaks something you carefully fixed in round 8. Everyone was watching the new change. Nobody was watching the old guarantee. And because the old fix had been working for twelve rounds, it wasn’t on anyone’s mind.

item.title: Field Notes on Reliable Agents (4): Deployed Is Not Executed
item.description:
There’s a specific flavor of self-deception that shows up once your changes get big enough to have plumbing. You write a feature. You deploy it. The deploy succeeds. You mark it done. And it never runs — not because it’s broken, but because nothing actually calls it on the path you care about.

I’ve shipped this bug enough times that I now treat “deployed” and “working” as unrelated facts until proven otherwise. This note is about the two ways the gap opens, and how to close each.

item.title: Field Notes on Reliable Agents (1): The Build Is the Only Gate
item.description:
Last month a three-agent run left me with a repo that would not compile, and every agent in it had reported success. That contradiction is the whole subject of this note.

The setup was ordinary. A parent agent split a refactor into three tasks and handed each to a child. Child A moved a shared type into a new module. Child B renamed a function that type referenced. Child C deleted a config field that, three files away, was still read. Each child ran tsc --noEmit on the files it had touched, saw no errors, and returned {"status": "done"}. The parent collected three “done"s and moved on.
